books.section: Topic 4.3 Politics and Regional Interests, C. A Temporary Truce on the Slavery Question in the Pre-Civil War Period

stimulus.text: A Republican campaign broadside map of the United States, published in 1856, colors free states and slave states differently and draws a line across the western territories labeled as the Missouri Compromise line. The territories beyond the line are marked as lands “whose destiny is yet to be decided.”
stimulus.source_note: Map of the United States, showing by colors the area of freedom and slavery, published by G. W. Elliott, New York, 1856 (Republican campaign broadside; scan of pre-1930 original). Public domain.

source: original; stimulus is an 1856 Republican campaign broadside map showing the Missouri Compromise line (public domain, in the shared image pool as 5s24-ch14-mcq-01)
stem: The line drawn across the western territories on this map is the line set by

options.text: the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, which doubled the country’s size
options.misconception: The Purchase bought the land; it set no line about slavery.

options.text: the Missouri Compromise of 1820, at 36°30′ north latitude
the Compromise of 1850, which settled the Mexican War lands
options.misconception: The Compromise of 1850 came thirty years later and set no such line across the Louisiana territory.
That act repealed the Missouri Compromise line; it did not draw it.

rationales.A: The Louisiana Purchase of 1803 doubled the country’s size, but it said nothing about where slavery could go. The line came later.
rationales.B: The map labels the line itself as the Missouri Compromise line, and the Compromise barred slavery north of 36°30′ in the Louisiana territory.
rationales.C: The Compromise of 1850 dealt with land won from Mexico, not the Louisiana territory, and it drew no 36°30′ line.
rationales.D: The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 let settlers decide slavery for themselves and repealed the line. A law that erases a line cannot be its source.
rationales.general:
1. Read the map’s own label. It calls the line the Missouri Compromise line.
2. Ask what the Compromise did. It barred slavery north of 36°30′ in the Louisiana territory.
3. Check the other laws. The Purchase bought land, the 1850 Compromise handled Mexican land, and Kansas-Nebraska repealed the line.
4. Put it together. Only the Missouri Compromise of 1820 drew this line.
Remember: a map’s labels are evidence too, so read them before you guess.
